stories.headline: How the middle classes came for business-class travel
stories.claim: Business class cabins are increasingly filled by leisure travellers, prompting questions about the future of the premium cabin.
stories.summary: A Telegraph travel feature argues that business class is losing its traditional corporate clientele to leisure passengers. Qantas reportedly said around 70 per cent of business cabin customers on London flights were leisure travellers, down from businesspeople once occupying as much as 90 per cent of seats. The piece says cheaper routes to upgrades, such as miles, loyalty schemes and seat auctions, have opened the cabin to families, retirees and holidaymakers. It also notes that some airlines are trimming amenities as the cabin democratises, while premium traffic still provides about a fifth of passenger revenue according to IATA. The article concludes that business class is unlikely to disappear soon.
key_points: Qantas reportedly said around 70 per cent of business cabin passengers on London flights are leisure travellers.

Companies are reluctant to spend heavily on premium travel amid tough economic conditions, and virtual meetings reduce travel needs.

Amenities are being trimmed in some cases, and premium economy growth is blurring class differences.
IATA data cited in the piece shows premium traffic is about a fifth of passenger revenue but only about 7 per cent of passenger miles.

stories.headline: A 930-megawatt reactor on the South African coast was cut to half power when dead sardines packed its seawater intake and a cooling pump shut itself off, the only nuclear plant in Africa was already down to one machine with its twin in refueling, and on Frida
stories.claim: Koeberg nuclear plant in South Africa was cut to half power in August after dead sardines blocked its seawater intake.
stories.summary: Eskom reduced Koeberg Unit 1, Africa's only nuclear plant, to 50 percent on August 21 after a cooling pump shut down when its seawater intake was blocked by dead sardines. Unit 2 was already offline for maintenance, so the plant briefly produced about a quarter of its normal output. Unit 1 returned to 70 percent by August 26, then tripped off the grid on August 27 for a cause Eskom said is under investigation. It was back online on August 31. The sardine die-off has been linked to pilchard herpesvirus, which the government says does not affect people.

stories.headline: Official data show China is dumping more U.S. Treasury debt. But it may actually be a stealth buyer, with a big stash suspiciously piling up in Canada
stories.claim: US data show China's Treasury holdings fell to $591bn, but analysts suspect Beijing holds more via non-US custodians.
stories.summary: US Treasury data show China's holdings of US Treasuries fell to $591 billion as of August, the lowest in 18 years and down from $700 billion a year earlier. The Treasury notes that the data is collected mainly from US-based custodians and may not reflect the true owners of securities held in overseas accounts. Analysts including Brad Setser argue that holdings in Canada, Belgium and European custodians have risen sharply, suggesting China may be using non-US custodians. Setser estimates China's US financial holdings remain between 50% and 55% of its reserves. China's trade surplus reached $938 billion in the first nine months of 2026, which could mean recycled dollars are still being invested in US assets.

stories.headline: Exclusive: NVIDIA’s Vera Team Says Chiplet Designs Sacrificed Single-Threaded Performance For Core Counts, And Agentic AI Is Now Forcing A Reversal
stories.claim: Nvidia's Vera team argues its Vera CPU is designed for agentic AI by combining high single-threaded speed with high throughput.
stories.summary: In an interview with Wccftech, members of Nvidia's Vera team explain why they think CPU design needs to change for agentic AI. They describe a shift from high single-core designs in the early 2010s, to chiplet-based many-core designs in the cloud era, which sacrificed single-threaded performance. Agentic AI requires rapid loops between CPU and GPU so expensive GPUs stay busy. Nvidia says Vera uses a monolithic compute die, custom LPDDR5X memory and a second-generation Scalable Coherent Fabric to deliver both high single-threaded performance and high throughput. The team also discusses disaggregation in AI infrastructure, comparing it with SK Hynix's proposed processing-in-SSD design.

stories.headline: ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
stories.claim: Housing and living-cost protests spread from Spain and France to Milan, Lisbon and Albania, with violence and arrests reported.
stories.summary: Protests over housing costs and living expenses have spread from Spain and France to Italy, Portugal and Albania. In Milan, a Saturday march turned violent, with about 50 people detained and at least two police officers injured. In Lisbon, protesters set up a tent camp in Rossio Square demanding action on housing. Italy's prime minister Giorgia Meloni blamed 'hooligans' for the violence, while Portugal's government said it understood public anger. Albania has seen violent demonstrations over university fees and calls for the prime minister's resignation.
key_points: A Saturday march in Milan over living costs turned violent, with masked rioters throwing stones and setting fire to barricades.
Police used water cannon and teargas in Milan; about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained and two officers injured.
In Lisbon, hundreds stayed overnight at a tent camp in Rossio Square, following a nationwide march of thousands.
Portuguese housing prices rose 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice the EU average, according to official data.
In Albania, protests over university conditions and tuition fees turned violent, with police using rubber bullets for the first time.
In Spain, a snap general election has been called for late November after housing measures were voted down in parliament.
stories.story:
Protests over the cost of living and housing have spread beyond Spain and France into Italy, Portugal and Albania, in some cases turning violent. In Milan, a march against rising living costs that began peacefully ended with masked people throwing stones and paving blocks at riot police and setting fire to barricades made of bar tables. Police responded with water cannon and teargas, and at least two officers were hurt. The LaPresse news agency reported about 50 detentions, many of those held being minors. Prime minister Giorgia Meloni said the right to protest did not extend to setting cities alight and accused hooligans of exploiting the demonstrations. Milan's centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said the grievances were understandable but the violence was not justifiable.

In Lisbon, a tent camp similar to one set up in Madrid weeks earlier appeared in Rossio Square after a nationwide march drew thousands. Protesters said they were struggling with rents and housing costs. Official data shows Portuguese housing prices rose 124% between 2015 and 2024, about twice the EU average. Portugal's prime minister, Luís Montenegro, said his government understood public frustration but warned rivals against importing unrest seen in France. A protest camp in Porto had already been set up earlier.

stories.story:
Andrew Left, a short seller whose securities fraud conviction was secured after a trial in Los Angeles, is seeking to have that verdict overturned. His lawyers argue that a witness, identified as Bachus, became caught up in an insider trading investigation, which they say calls the conviction into question.

According to court filings, the prosecution told Left's lawyers that it did not learn about the investigation until after the trial had finished. It is not clear which government agency opened the probe, or when Bachus or Grand Canyon Education became aware of it. Many of the relevant documents remain sealed or redacted on the court docket.

Justice Department prosecutors have pushed back. They say Left's lawyers overstated Bachus's part in the case, which involved alleged securities fraud linked to more than a dozen public companies. Prosecutors argued that Left wanted to carry out his own 'shadow investigation' into Bachus to discredit him, and said the law does not allow fishing expeditions in search of a claim.

Left declined to comment. His attorney, Eric S. Rosen, said he could not comment because key documents remain under seal. A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in Los Angeles also declined to comment. The next steps will depend on how the court handles the sealed material and whether it accepts the argument that the undisclosed probe affects the verdict.

stories.headline: Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
stories.claim: Rubio says Ukraine currently lacks access to Starshield, with a request for deep-strike use still under discussion, and denies Starlink was deliberately disrupted.
stories.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Ukraine does not currently have access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, but its request to use it for deep strikes inside Russia is under discussion. He denied that a reported Starlink disruption in Ukraine was deliberate or ordered by the White House. Zelenskyy had suggested the disruption was deliberate and said satellites were not tracking fast-moving drone antennas. Rubio also defended the US decision to waive sanctions on Russia and buyers of its oil and gas.

Ukraine has asked for access to use it for deep strikes inside Russia, and the request is under discussion.

stories.story:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Ukraine does not currently have access to Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service. He said a Ukrainian request to use the system for attacks deep inside Russia is being discussed. Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Rubio stressed that Starlink is a commercial product, while Starshield is a defence product used mainly by US defence agencies and other government partners.

The remarks followed reports of a disruption to Starlink services in Ukraine. Zelenskyy suggested the disruption was deliberate and said the satellites were not tracking antennas on objects moving faster than about 100 miles per hour, which he said affected Ukrainian drones defending against Russian jet-powered drones. Rubio rejected the suggestion, saying it was not deliberate and that no one at the White House had ordered speeds to be reduced. He said the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level and called the reports 'categorically false'.

The dispute comes as President Donald Trump faces criticism from both Democrats and Republicans for waiving sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas. The waiver came days before restrictions were due to take effect under a law Trump signed last month. Zelenskyy said on social media that financial relief for Vladimir Putin would only encourage further attacks and urged Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow.

The episode highlights Ukraine's reliance on commercial and military satellite communications in a conflict now in its fifth year. Ukrainian officials had said last week that Starlink restrictions had slowed some drones. Whether Washington agrees to grant Starshield access for deep strikes remains unresolved, and the sanctions waiver is likely to remain a source of political debate in the US and Ukraine.
stories.market_take: Mainly a geopolitical and policy story; SpaceX is private, so no listed Starlink exposure, though sanctions waivers could influence energy markets.

stocks.reason: A sanctions waiver on Russian oil and gas buyers could ease supply concerns and weigh on prices.

stories.story:
Arizona has joined Nevada in its legal battle against Trump administration proposals to cut the states' shares of the Colorado River. The move, reported by The Guardian, follows restrictions announced by the interior department this summer. Those restrictions could substantially reduce water delivered to the lower basin states of Arizona, California and Nevada over the next two years, depending on the river's condition.

The river's two main reservoirs, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, have fallen to historically low levels because of heavy use and a changing climate. States sharing the river have been unable to agree on how to share the shortage, and missed several deadlines for a consensus. The federal government then stepped in. The upper basin states of Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico were exempted from the cuts, which lower basin leaders have sharply criticised.

Arizona governor Katie Hobbs said the state was drawing a line and taking legal action because the federal government was not holding the upper basin accountable for water it says it is owed. Tom Buschatzke, director of Arizona's water department, said the intervention was needed to protect Arizona's legal rights while keeping open a route to a collaborative deal with California and Nevada. The interior department had not immediately responded to a request for comment.

The dispute could go on for some time. The main fear is that if reservoir levels fall far enough, water might no longer reach downstream, a situation known as deadpool. Further court filings and any revised agreement among the states will show how the legal fight develops.
stories.market_take: Water cuts could affect agriculture and utilities in the Southwest, though the direct effect on listed companies is likely limited.

The waiver was made by executive order on Friday, just before a sanctions law passed in September was due to take effect. Lawmakers from both parties criticised the move, and Ukraine's president said it rewards Vladimir Putin. Rubio linked the decision to energy price pressures from the Iran war and Houthi attacks, and to a deal allowing Russian diesel exports.
key_points: Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia for 60 days.

stories.story:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that President Donald Trump's decision to waive sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause. He said the period would allow the administration to analyse what imposing the measures would mean for the global economy and the US economy. Rubio noted that the restrictions involved several countries, not only Russia.

The waiver was set out in an executive order Trump signed late on Friday. It exempted Russia from measures passed by Congress in September, which included sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and gave the president power to sanction major buyers of Russian oil and gas. The law was due to take effect two days after the waiver. Trump said late on Saturday the decision would be good for the country, though it was unclear whether he had finalised his position.

The move drew sharp criticism from lawmakers of both parties. Republican senator Thom Tillis called it irresponsible and said the Iran problem was the real route to lower energy prices. Ted Cruz called it a mistake. Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky said he feared more sanctions would be lifted and that the decision rewarded Putin. The waiver came after Trump struck a deal with Putin to allow Russian diesel exports in return for easing sanctions.

Rubio framed the decision around energy markets, citing the US war on Iran and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as pressures on global oil and diesel prices. Diesel costs are feeding into the US economy ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, where cost of living is a major concern for voters. The longer-term effect will depend on whether the pause is extended or the sanctions are reimposed when it ends.

stories.story:
Around 300 people gathered in Atlanta on Saturday for a 'No Kings' rally, one of many held across the United States the same day. The event was framed by organisers as a push to get people to vote in the November 3 midterm elections and to protect democracy, rather than a large-scale protest. Participants marched about a mile from Piedmont Park to St. Mark's church, where volunteers were invited to sign up.

Speakers included Kelsea Bond, a labour organiser and Atlanta city councillor who is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. She argued that the economy should serve working people and criticised Georgia's Republican leaders for rolling back voting rights. Her remarks reflected concern over a possible return of redistricting in the state, after Georgia's Republican legislative leaders rejected a bid in June, partly out of fear of a voter backlash.

Protesters voiced opposition to a range of Trump policies. Many criticised the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and others objected to the war in Iran, citing rising prices and inflation. One banner depicted Trump and Vladimir Putin in a Russian doll format, reflecting anger over foreign policy. The atmosphere was described as defiant but peaceful, with families and children present and police holding back traffic.

The 'No Kings' movement began in 2025 after an AI-generated image of Trump as a monarch circulated. Earlier protests drew large crowds in major cities, but organisers said this weekend's approach was deliberately smaller and community-based, sending people to polling places with their neighbours. The midterms are widely seen as a test of public opinion on the president's record and cost-of-living concerns.

stories.headline: Indigenous woman shackled to hospital bed while in labour in Queensland
stories.claim: An incarcerated Indigenous woman was reportedly shackled to a hospital bed while in labour in Queensland, prompting calls for a national ban.
stories.summary: An advocacy group says an incarcerated Aboriginal woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while giving birth by caesarean section to a premature baby. The disclosure came days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a Senate bill that would have banned shackling incarcerated women during childbirth. Queensland corrective services says the incident will be internally reviewed. Senator Lidia Thorpe, who introduced the bill, says the federal government should act.
key_points: Sisters Inside says an Aboriginal woman was shackled on and off after arriving at hospital following a premature caesarean birth.
Hospital staff reportedly asked for the restraints to be removed, but prison staff refused until Friday.
Queensland corrective services says restraints are only used as a last resort and the incident will be reviewed.
Labor and the Coalition blocked Lidia Thorpe's bill to ban shackling of pregnant prisoners during childbirth.
The federal government says criminal justice is a matter for states and territories.

stories.story:
An advocacy group has said that an incarcerated Aboriginal woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend. Debbie Kilroy, chief executive of Sisters Inside, said the woman gave birth by caesarean section to a premature baby and had been shackled on and off since arriving at hospital. She said hospital staff had tried to have the restraints removed and had called her organisation, with some staff reportedly crying because prison staff would not take them off. The shackles were reportedly removed on Friday, by which point Kilroy said the woman's health had been deteriorating.

The case emerged just days before Labor and the Coalition voted down a Senate bill, introduced by independent senator Lidia Thorpe, that would ban shackling incarcerated women during childbirth and stop children being strip-searched. An inquiry into the bill heard of women having one leg and one arm shackled, leaving only one arm free to hold a newborn. Australia has signed the UN Bangkok Rules, which state that restraints should never be used on women during labour, birth or immediately after birth.

Queensland Corrective Services said the incident would be subject to an internal review and that restraints are only used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners where needed for public safety. The Coalition said it understood the intent of the bill but would not support it. Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr said he was deeply concerned and would raise the matter with the Queensland attorney general.

Thorpe criticised the federal government for leaving the issue to the states and territories, arguing the Commonwealth has the constitutional power to set a national standard. The review of the Queensland case and any further federal debate on the issue are likely to follow.

Schools have closed in parts of the region, and air quality in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur and Dili has been rated very hazardous by IQAir. Indonesia has also dispersed 2.4 tonnes of dry ice by plane at a South Sumatra airport to try to disperse the haze.

Environmental group Auriga says more than 637,000 hectares burned from January to August, while the deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas puts the figure near 900,000 hectares. The fires are concentrated on Borneo and Sumatra, where dense forests and peatland are especially prone to burning in the dry season. A severe 'super-El Nino' weather pattern has added heat and dryness, allowing the fires to spread faster. Residents describe effects on health, income and daily routines, with some workers saying they cannot stop working despite the smoke.

Singapore said it would issue warnings to seven Indonesian companies it has identified as responsible for the fires. The Philippines, which holds the ASEAN chair, said the haze would be raised at upcoming meetings before a November ASEAN summit in Manila. Residents in Malaysia and elsewhere have called for regional action, and the ASEAN alert reflects that the problem is recurring; the centre has already issued two Level 3 alerts this year. The episode is likely to keep pressure on regional governments over enforcement and cross-border pollution.

stories.claim: Strathclyde Pension Fund reports a record £12bn surplus and is cutting employer contributions.

The fund is cutting employer contributions from 17.5 to 6.5 per cent for two years, saving about £500m a year. Critics say the surplus should be spent on public services, while the Treasury says the Local Government Pension Scheme will only fund pensions. The debate comes ahead of the chancellor's first Budget.

stories.story:
Strathclyde Pension Fund, which is administered by Glasgow City Council, has reported a funding surplus of about £12bn. Its latest accounts show that it holds £12bn more than it needs to pay the pensions of its near-300,000 members, and the surplus is believed to be the largest ever recorded in a UK-based retirement scheme. The fund holds £33bn of assets and is the largest of 86 council pension funds within the £550bn Local Government Pension Scheme. Strathclyde estimates its funding level at 158 per cent of its liabilities.

The fund says it will use the surplus to cut employer contributions from 17.5 per cent to 6.5 per cent for the next two years, which it estimates will save employers around £500m a year. Analysts suggest the wider LGPS has excess funds of at least £150bn, and council taxpayers contribute a small share of the roughly £10bn employers pay in each year.

Critics, including former pensions minister Ros Altmann, argue that the surplus is being wasted and should instead help councils fund services such as potholes, bins and social care, or be used to give employers a contribution holiday. Professor John Clancy of Birmingham City University said the money is effectively taxpayers' money and that pension funds should be more open about it. The article notes that the surplus is similar to the estimated headroom the UK as a whole has ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget in ten days.

The Treasury has dismissed suggestions that the government will raid the scheme again. A recent £500m drawn from the LGPS helped fund a 3.5 per cent teachers' pay rise that averted strike action, but the Treasury said the scheme 'will only be used to fund pensions'. The debate over who owns pension surpluses is likely to continue as the Budget approaches.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; the Budget debate on public finances and pension surpluses may attract attention from gilt and UK financial markets.

The National Medicines and Poisons Board says only eight of the 30 factories in Khartoum that closed during the conflict have resumed production, even as security in the capital has improved. That has increased reliance on imports, which are costlier because of the currency's slide.

The report underlines how the conflict has moved from a battlefield crisis into a daily struggle for basic healthcare. The article describes ongoing violence in North Kordofan as well. For the wider world, it shows how a collapsing currency and damaged supply chains can turn manageable chronic conditions into life-threatening ones. No market implications are discussed.

stories.headline: Funeral held for 75 Palestinians after remains recovered from Gaza ruins
stories.claim: A mass funeral was held in Gaza for 75 Palestinians whose remains were recovered from rubble in Daraj.
stories.summary: A mass funeral was held in Gaza City for 75 Palestinians whose remains were recovered from the rubble of homes in the Daraj neighbourhood. The Gaza Civil Defence says it believes remains of about 8,000 more people are still under rubble. Recovery is hampered by a lack of equipment.
key_points: Remains of 75 Palestinians were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery on Sunday.
Most victims were from the Daraj neighbourhood of northeastern Gaza City.
The Civil Defence says remains of about 8,000 more people are still trapped.
Recovery efforts face shortages of equipment and heavy machinery.
At least 74,475 Palestinians have been killed since the war began in October 2023, according to the report.
stories.story:
A mass funeral has been held in Gaza for 75 Palestinians whose remains were found under the rubble of destroyed homes. The burial took place at the Sheikh Radwan Cemetery on Sunday morning, with hundreds of people attending the procession, according to Al Jazeera. The Ministry of Health announced the funeral.

Most of the victims came from the Daraj neighbourhood in northeastern Gaza City. Al Jazeera's correspondent said most of the remains belonged to women and children who were inside their homes when the buildings were struck. The remains included body parts and personal belongings, and were wrapped in Palestinian flags before burial.

Abdullah al-Majdalawi, of Gaza's Civil Defence, said the remains were recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes and belonged to about 20 families. He said the buildings were bombed in the early months of the war and that recovery work is severely hampered by a lack of equipment and heavy machinery. The Civil Defence began a second phase of recovery operations in July, and says it believes the remains of around 8,000 more Palestinians remain under rubble across Gaza.

The UN agency UNRWA estimates that about 200,000 buildings in Gaza are damaged or destroyed. The report cites a death toll of at least 74,475 Palestinians since Israel launched its military campaign in October 2023. Al Jazeera describes the campaign as genocidal, a characterisation Israel rejects; the International Court of Justice is separately hearing a genocide case against Israel.

stories.headline: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
stories.claim: Zack Polanski says he will not overturn the Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion, which stays policy until 2028.
stories.summary: Green Party leader Zack Polanski said he will not try to overturn the conference motion describing Zionism as a form of racism. He says he wants to amend it, but party rules mean that cannot happen until 2028. The motion has caused a major backlash, including from Labour, which threatens to end council power-sharing.
key_points: The motion passed 1,022 to 813 at the Green conference in Brighton earlier this month.
Polanski says it stays policy until 2028 because of party rules.
He wants to amend it to focus on Israelis and Palestinians deciding the future.
Labour says it will end council power-sharing with Greens unless councillors disown the motion.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission has asked the party for more information.
stories.story:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he will not try to overturn a motion passed by party members that describes Zionism as a form of racism. Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he said he would like to amend the motion, but under party rules it will remain policy until 2028.

The motion was passed at the party's conference in Brighton earlier this month by 1,022 votes to 813, a small share of the party's roughly 230,000 members. It describes Zionism in terms of an ethnonationalist Jewish state and backs a single democratic state across historic Palestine, a full arms embargo on Israel and Palestinian liberation. Polanski said he would not have voted for it without two amendments, both of which were defeated at conference.

The motion has caused a fortnight of criticism across the political spectrum. The Equality and Human Rights Commission has asked the party for more information to assess whether parts could be discriminatory under the 2010 Equality Act. The Board of Deputies of British Jews called it an attack on the Jewish community. Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with Green council groups unless councillors disown the motion, and some Green MPs want the party's decision-making procedures reviewed.

Asked whether Zionism is racist, Polanski said the practical application of Zionism had come at the cost of Palestinians and described the Israeli-Palestinian situation in strong terms. He said no Jewish Green members would be excluded because of their faith or background, and that being Jewish and supporting Israel are separate things. The row overshadowed the final days of his campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where he came second to Labour, and has raised questions about his leadership.

stories.headline: Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season in West Bank?
stories.claim: EU and several governments condemn Israeli settler attacks on diplomats and Palestinians during the West Bank olive harvest.
stories.summary: The European Union and several European governments have condemned a series of Israeli settler attacks in the occupied West Bank, including an assault on diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland and on a French mayor. The attacks came during the Palestinian olive harvest, which has seen settler violence surge in recent weeks. The EU called for accountability and an end to settlement expansion. Critics say condemnations without sanctions have not stopped the violence. The US Secretary of State also said he was disturbed by the attack on an American photojournalist.
key_points: Settlers attacked vehicles of French, Belgian and Polish diplomats near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh on Saturday.
A French mayor, Bernard Baudoux, was thrown to the ground and assaulted, and a Belgian consulate vehicle window was smashed.
An American freelance photojournalist for The Washington Post was attacked on Friday, prompting comment from Marco Rubio.
The EU said it expects full accountability and urged Israel to halt settlement expansion.
Israeli police have opened an investigation, and settler violence this olive season has reportedly exceeded 2025 totals.
Critics, including a former EU representative, say EU ministers have not agreed sanctions on violent settlers.
stories.story:
Israeli settler attacks in the occupied West Bank have drawn sharp international condemnation after a weekend of violence during the Palestinian olive harvest. On Saturday, at least seven masked settlers surrounded diplomatic vehicles from France, Belgium and Poland near the village of Taybeh, demanded identification, smashed a window of a Belgian consulate car and assaulted a visiting French mayor. The attack came a day after settlers attacked Palestinian olive pickers and an American photojournalist, Heidi Levine, who writes for The Washington Post.

The European Union issued a statement calling for full accountability and effective measures to stop violence against Palestinians and journalists during the harvest. It also urged Israel to follow international humanitarian and human rights law and to stop expanding settlements. Foreign ministers from Belgium, France and elsewhere voiced their own concern. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration was very disturbed by the images and urged Israel to crack down on the violence. Israeli police have opened an investigation into the assault on the French mayor.

The article reports that settler attacks this harvest season have already surpassed the 2025 totals. Earlier on Saturday, settlers reportedly injured six Palestinians in Ma'in village, and Israeli forces opened fire on farmers in Deir Ammar, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society. Palestinian and former EU officials argued that statements alone are insufficient. A former EU representative noted that at an October 12 meeting, EU foreign ministers were still unable to agree on sanctions against violent settlers.

What happens next depends on whether Israeli authorities act on arrests and whether EU member states move from statements to sanctions. The harvest season continues, so further incidents are likely to test those responses.

sources.name: Al Jazeera
sources.title: Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season in West Bank?

stories.headline: Is FIFA scrapping its peace prize after awarding it to US President Trump?
stories.claim: FIFA Council members are questioning and may scrap the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to Donald Trump.
stories.summary: Several FIFA Council members reportedly want the Peace Prize awarded to Donald Trump scrapped or reformed. A committee will assess the award and report before the council meeting on December 16. The move follows criticism of FIFA president Gianni Infantino and the award's links to politics.
key_points: Several FIFA members called for the discontinuation of the award at the Zurich council meeting.
FIFA's Football Social Responsibility Committee will assess the prize and make a recommendation.
A decision is expected at the next FIFA Council meeting in Doha on December 16.
Critics include the Norwegian FA, a human rights group complaint, and players such as Jackson Irvine.
stories.story:
FIFA's governing council is reconsidering the FIFA Peace Prize, which was given to US President Donald Trump at the World Cup 2026 draw in Washington. According to the report, several member nations asked at a council meeting in Zurich for the award to be discontinued, and others said it should no longer go to politicians. FIFA has tasked its 22-member Football Social Responsibility Committee with reviewing the prize and proposing next steps before the council meets in Doha on December 16. Debbie Hewitt, a FIFA vice president, said the review would examine how the prize came about and who made the decision.

The award was created in November of last year and presented to Trump in December. Critics say it blurs the line between sport and politics, and it has drawn complaints from the Norwegian Football Association, a human rights group that filed an ethics complaint against Infantino, and Australian player Jackson Irvine. Infantino has said the committee will analyse the award and that a decision will be taken at the next council meeting. He has previously said Trump should have won the Nobel Peace Prize.

The article notes that the award was announced shortly after a US strike in the Caribbean and that the US and Israel later went to war with Iran. Infantino also faces criticism over a World Cup ticket sale plan and calls for his removal. The next step is the committee's recommendation, which could lead to the award being scrapped, reformed or kept as it is.
stories.market_take: Little direct market impact expected; the story concerns sports governance.

stories.headline: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale’s UK data centre weeks before its IPO
stories.claim: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, ahead of Nscale's IPO.
stories.summary: The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The move comes as the AI cloud startup prepares an IPO seeking up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. Microsoft has not commented, and the site has faced grid connection delays. The story also covers wider investor caution around neocloud firms.
key_points: The Telegraph reports Microsoft has walked away from anchoring Nscale's Loughton data centre, with no reason given.
Authorities have reportedly told Nscale that power may not arrive until the 2030s.
Nscale is seeking up to $3bn in an IPO as soon as this month.
Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of Nscale's contracts, per its IPO filing.
Nscale says the Microsoft relationship is strong and the grid issue does not affect its other contracts.
CoreWeave shares fell 25% last week, reflecting wariness toward neocloud firms.
stories.story:
The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor the first British data centre of Nscale, the AI cloud startup, in Loughton, Essex. The move comes as Nscale prepares to go public, and Bloomberg, citing the Telegraph, says the site has faced a series of delays. The Telegraph did not give a reason for Microsoft's decision. Microsoft did not comment to the Telegraph and did not immediately respond to Bloomberg.

The Loughton site has been affected by grid problems. Authorities have reportedly told Nscale not to expect a power supply until the 2030s. The Next Web had reported in July that the grid could not connect the site in time for its planned opening. Nscale says it remains committed to the site, is looking at other power sources and UK locations, and that its relationship with Microsoft is strong and long-term. It says the grid issue does not affect its other contracts.

The IPO is significant. Nscale is seeking to raise as much as $3bn, possibly as soon as this month. Its filing shows Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts. Anthropic agreed in August to spend $45bn on Nscale compute over six years, and Microsoft has signed a letter of intent for a campus in West Virginia. Bloomberg also reports that Nscale's flagship Norway site is six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts of a planned 30-megawatt facility running.

The wider context is investor caution about neocloud companies, which are racing to build AI computing capacity and often borrow heavily. CoreWeave shares fell 25% last week, their worst week since November, and Australia's Firmus scrapped its IPO after failing to win enough support. Whether Microsoft's withdrawal is confirmed, and how Nscale's listing is priced, will be closely watched.

stories.headline: Apple’s next HomeView could debut as soon as next year with a robotic arm: report
stories.claim: Apple may release a higher-end HomeView model with a larger screen and motorised arm as early as 2027 or 2028, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
stories.summary: Citing Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, 9to5Mac reports that Apple is working on a more advanced HomeView smart display, code-named J595, planned for 2027 or 2028. It would have a roughly 9-inch screen and a motorised arm allowing a full 360-degree swivel with voice-based tracking of speakers. It would sit above the existing $299 model rather than replace it. The timing and features are reported plans, not an Apple announcement.
key_points: The reported model is code-named J595 and is planned for 2027 or 2028.
It would have a roughly 9-inch screen, up from 7 inches on the current HomeView.
A motorised arm would let the display turn a full 360 degrees toward the speaker.
It would be a higher-end option and not replace the $299 HomeView.
Apple has not confirmed these plans.
stories.story:
Apple has launched its HomeView smart home display, priced at $299, and 9to5Mac reports that a more advanced version may follow. Citing Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the report says Apple is developing a model code-named J595, which could arrive in 2027 or 2028. The article suggests the product, possibly named HomeView Pro, has been delayed by the difficulty of building a smarter Siri.

According to the reported details, the higher-end model would have a screen of roughly 9 inches, compared with 7 inches on the current device. A motorised robotic arm would let the display swivel a full 360 degrees, and voice recognition would be used to identify the speaker and turn toward them. The product is described as a premium option that would not replace the existing model, so it would not be sold at the same $299 price.

Gurman is a well-established Bloomberg reporter who covers Apple and has a generally strong record on product plans, though timelines often shift. The report is therefore credible but still unconfirmed, and Apple has not commented on the device. The timeline is more than a year away, which adds uncertainty.

If the plans proceed, the product could be relevant to Apple's smart home strategy and to suppliers of displays and small robotics components. The effect on investors would be modest and would depend on how the wider product line performs. Readers should treat the details as provisional.

signals: Timeline 2027-2028, long-range and subject to change
stories.market_take: A reported premium smart display could add modest upside for Apple's hardware lineup, but the launch is far off.

stories.headline: The reason your Amazon Alexa devices are always listening
stories.claim: Explainer on how Amazon Alexa devices listen for wake words and how users can limit recording and delete voice data.
stories.summary: Engadget explains that Alexa devices listen locally for acoustic patterns matching their wake word and only record and send audio once it is detected, according to Amazon. It gives practical steps for privacy, including muting the microphone and changing voice recording retention to three months, 18 months, until deleted, or not at all. The piece notes that deletion settings apply only to Amazon's cloud and do not cover third-party devices.
key_points: Alexa devices listen for acoustic patterns that match the wake word rather than transcribing everything.
Audio is recorded and sent to the cloud only after the wake word is recognised, according to Amazon.
Users can mute the microphone with the button on Echo devices, shown by a red light.
Voice recording retention can be set to three months, 18 months, until deleted, or not kept at all.
Deleting data does not affect third-party devices and may reduce personalisation.
stories.story:
Engadget has published an explainer on whether Amazon Alexa devices are always listening. The article notes that more than 600 million Alexa-enabled devices have been sold worldwide, and that Amazon has recently announced several new products, including a new line of tablets, that use Alexa. The piece addresses a common privacy concern about devices that sit in homes and respond to voice.

According to Amazon, Alexa does not transcribe every word. Instead, it listens for acoustic patterns that match its wake word. Only after recognising that wake word does the device begin active listening, record audio and send it to the cloud. The article compares this to hearing one's name in a conversation without catching every other word.

The explainer then sets out options for users. The simplest is to press the microphone-off button on Echo devices, which shows a red light. Users who prefer voice activation can change their recording settings in the Alexa app to keep recordings for three months or 18 months, keep them until deleted, or not retain them at all. Some devices allow deletion by voice, although this does not work on Alexa+ or Amazon Kids devices.

The article stresses that these settings apply only to Amazon's cloud. Third-party devices, such as some robotic vacuums or smart TVs, may still hold data. Deleting voice recordings can also reduce how well Alexa personalises responses, because it cannot keep a voice profile. The piece is consumer guidance rather than a new development, and it has no clear market implications.

sources.title: The reason your Amazon Alexa devices are always listening

stories.headline: Air Force officer killed in rappelling accident before UTSA’s game against Navy
stories.claim: An Air Force officer died after falling from the Alamodome rafters during a rappelling demonstration before a UTSA game.
stories.summary: An unnamed US Air Force officer fell from the rafters of the Alamodome in San Antonio while rappelling before UTSA's home game against Navy on Saturday. He was treated on the field, taken to hospital and later died. Nellis Air Force Base said he was with the 6th Combat Training Squadron. The game start was delayed by about 10 minutes, and UTSA expressed condolences. This is a tragic local news story with no market relevance.
key_points: An Air Force officer fell from the Alamodome rafters during a Salute to Armed Forces event.
He was treated on the field, taken away on a stretcher and died later at a local hospital.
Nellis Air Force Base said he was part of the 6th Combat Training Squadron.
The game was delayed by around 10 minutes; UTSA said it was deeply saddened.
stories.story:
An Air Force officer has died after falling from the rafters of the Alamodome in San Antonio, Texas, before the University of Texas at San Antonio's home game against Navy on Saturday. The officer had been taking part in an event marking UTSA's Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans night when he fell while rappelling down from the stadium rafters onto the field.

He was treated on the field and taken away on a stretcher, then died later at a local hospital. Nellis Air Force Base said he was part of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, a unit that trains military members in rappelling from helicopters. The officer has not been publicly named in the report.

The incident was captured on video, which showed the crowd reacting as he fell. The Alamodome roof sits around 170 feet above the field. The start of the game was delayed by about 10 minutes. UTSA coach Jeff Traylor said the mood in the stadium changed sharply afterwards, and the university said its thoughts were with the officer, his family and his military colleagues.

The event is a reminder of the risks in staged military displays at large public events. No further details about the cause of the fall were given in the report.

stories.story:
At least one person was killed and at least five were injured in an overnight drone attack on St Petersburg, which hit two oil facilities: the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot. Regional governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being put out. The attack also struck a logistics centre belonging to the e-commerce firm Ozon and a regional data centre of the social network VK. Twelve apartment buildings and two homes were damaged, Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed, and mobile internet disruption was possible. Kyiv had not commented at the time of reporting.

The attack comes after a short-lived pause. Ukraine had stopped striking Russian oil facilities for three days after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire last week. Ukraine says Russia continued attacks on its energy sector, and Zelensky said Russia had targeted it 76 times since the ceasefire was announced. Ukraine then resumed its strikes earlier this week, which drew criticism from Trump. Russia's defence ministry said it had downed over 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight into Sunday.

The wider context includes a US deal to import Russian diesel, intended to lower US fuel prices that have risen during the Iran conflict ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky has said the deal amounts to the US investing in Russia's war effort, and Trump's decision to suspend some sanctions on Russia has drawn criticism, including from some Republicans. Both sides have been hitting each other's energy infrastructure ahead of winter, and the UN said the first two weeks of October were the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.

Russian strikes have left hundreds of thousands without power, and Zelensky said tens of thousands were still without electricity. The attack coincided with the opening of Putin's flagship economic forum. Earlier this month Ukraine also attacked Yandex, causing disruption. Whether the energy truce holds, and how Moscow responds, remains to be seen.

stories.headline: Researchers train AI to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals
stories.claim: Swedish Defence Research Agency researchers built WiFireNet, an experimental AI that spots concealed handguns from Wi-Fi signal distortion.
stories.summary: Researchers at the Swedish Defence Research Agency (FOI) have developed WiFireNet, an experimental AI system that attempts to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals rather than cameras or metal detectors. The method analyses channel state information, the way an object alters ambient Wi-Fi as it passes through or reflects signals. In controlled indoor trials the system reached an average handgun-detection precision of 72.5%, falling to 53.8% under stricter location requirements. The team has released its code, models and dataset as open source, while privacy critics warn about the lack of regulation for Wi-Fi sensing.
key_points: FOI researchers posted a paper on arXiv describing WiFireNet, a system that detects concealed handguns from Wi-Fi signal data.
The system uses a transmitter, a receiver and a deep learning model that reads channel state information.
Average handgun-detection precision was 72.5% in trials with up to four moving people, but fell to 53.8% when exact weapon location was required.
Performance drops in unfamiliar indoor layouts, and the prototype used the 1999 802.11a standard.
Future phases plan to use Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 with higher-resolution data.
Critics warn that Wi-Fi sensing raises privacy concerns in the absence of regulatory frameworks.
stories.story:
Researchers at the Swedish Defence Research Agency (FOI) have described an experimental artificial intelligence system that aims to identify concealed handguns by analysing how people and objects disturb ordinary Wi-Fi signals. The work was detailed in a paper posted on arXiv on 13 October. The system, named WiFireNet, is positioned as a non-intrusive alternative to visible cameras and metal detectors, which the researchers describe as either conspicuous or cumbersome.

The approach relies on channel state information, the data describing how an object changes Wi-Fi signals through reflection and penetration depending on its shape, orientation and material. To train the model, the team built a dataset called the WiFire Dataset by recording video of people walking with objects, from phones to handguns, while simultaneously capturing Wi-Fi signals. They included a plastic handgun, a metal water bottle, a real metal handgun and a phone so the system could tell a gun apart from similar everyday items.

In controlled trials with up to four moving people in a small indoor space, the system reached an average handgun-detection precision of 72.5%. When the task required pinpointing the weapon's exact position on a person, precision dropped to 53.8%. The neural network also struggled in unfamiliar indoor layouts that it had not been tested on. The researchers stress that the system is still experimental and the prototype used an old wireless standard to prove the concept.

The team has made the code, models and dataset open source to encourage further work, and plans to move to modern Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 networks with richer data. The article notes that Wi-Fi sensing is becoming more popular as a surveillance technique because it needs little specialised equipment. Critics argue that its spread, together with the absence of regulatory frameworks, raises serious privacy concerns. The results suggest the technology is far from ready for real-world security use, though it marks a notable research step.

stories.headline: DJI’s first battery-swapping dock gets drones recharged and back in the air in under 45 seconds
stories.claim: DJI has launched the Dock 4 battery-swapping drone dock, paired with the Matrice 5TD, which is not sold in the US.
stories.summary: DJI has unveiled the Dock 4, a drone dock that swaps batteries automatically in about 25 seconds, allowing a drone to be back in the air within 45 seconds of landing. It is aimed at emergency response, which DJI calls dock-as-a-first-responder. The dock works only with the new Matrice 5TD drone and is not FCC-authorised or sold in the US. Chinese partners are taking orders for a kit priced at 167,999 yuan, about $25,000 for the hardware alone. The launch comes amid a US regulatory crackdown on foreign-made drones.
key_points: The Dock 4 swaps drone batteries in about 25 seconds, with a turnaround of under 45 seconds from landing to takeoff.
Each battery pack is rated at 260 Wh and can be charged from 15% to 95% in roughly 27 minutes.
The dock works only with the Matrice 5TD drone and the DJI O4 Ground Station.
The Matrice 5TD carries high-resolution cameras, thermal sensors, LiDAR and a laser rangefinder.
The kit is priced at 167,999 yuan, about $25,000, and is available through Chinese partners.

stories.story:
DJI, the Chinese drone maker, has launched the Dock 4, a battery-swapping drone dock that it says is its first product of this kind. According to a company press release, the dock replaces a drone's battery automatically in about 25 seconds, so the aircraft can take off again within 45 seconds of landing. Without battery swapping, a normal recharge would take around 30 minutes. DJI markets the product for emergency response, calling it a dock-as-a-first-responder solution.

The dock can charge two battery packs at once, each rated at 260 Wh, and estimates say each can be charged from 15% to 95% in about 27 minutes. The packs can also provide backup power for the dock, and with at least two packs loaded the dock can keep swapping batteries during a grid power cut. The dock weighs 66 kg without accessories. It works only with the new Matrice 5TD drone, which carries three 50 MP cameras, thermal sensors, LiDAR, radar and a laser rangefinder, and it can detect 17 types of object.

The kit is available to order from DJI partners in China at 167,999 yuan, roughly $25,000 for the hardware alone. However, the product is not FCC-authorised and cannot be sold in the United States. In December last year the FCC added all foreign-made drones and their critical components to its Covered List, which blocks new models from authorisation unless a US agency certifies they pose no security risk. DJI has sued the commission this year. A separate FCC proposal from August could also remove previously authorised foreign drones with LiDAR or thermal sensors from sale, though no final order had been issued as of 17 October.

The launch underlines how DJI is pushing into automated drone operations for public safety while its US access is restricted. Whether the dock gains a meaningful foothold will depend on how the regulatory dispute develops and on demand from customers outside the US.
stories.market_take: Limited direct effect on listed companies, though US restrictions on DJI's products remain a background risk for drone supply chains.

stories.story:
MapQuest, the long-running online mapping and navigation service, has released an app update that adds a feature called the Surveillance Layer. The company announced the change on Bluesky. When the layer is switched on in the map options, it shows the locations of known automatic licence plate readers, which are cameras that read vehicle registration plates. Licence plate readers are widely used by police and cities, which say they help track suspected criminals and improve public safety. Critics, however, describe them as a serious privacy intrusion, pointing to cases where officers misused the systems and to administrative errors, including one that led to an innocent car reviewer being detained. The article also mentions a Canadian YouTuber who built a camera that tracked police vehicles, and whose efforts drew a visit from officers who raised privacy concerns.

Police departments previously objected when Waze added a feature in 2015 that let users report officers' locations, so there may be pushback against MapQuest's move as well. stories.claim: Researchers show that a Cyrillic-based lookalike of apple.com can evade Chromium's typosquatting protections.

The trick relies on a Cyrillic character, ө, which is not on Chromium's list of 29 confusable Cyrillic characters. The article explains how Chromium's rules work and where they fall short. It concludes that companies should register lookalike domains and encourage passkeys, which are bound to specific domains.
key_points: The domain аррӏө.com evades Chromium's protections because the character ө is not on its list of 29 confusable Cyrillic characters.
Chromium shows Punycode for mixed-alphabet lookalikes and blocks all-Cyrillic lookalikes from the list.

stories.story:
Tom's Hardware reports on research by Have I Been Squatted, which shows that typosquatting attacks using internationalised domain names remain viable. The researchers used the domain аррӏө.com, which looks like apple.com but is not identical to it, to show that a specific combination of Cyrillic characters can slip past several layers of protection in Chromium-based browsers.

The weakness is subtle. Chromium blocks domains that mix alphabets, displaying them in Punycode instead, and it also keeps a list of 29 Cyrillic characters that closely resemble Latin letters. Using only those characters is blocked. The character ө, however, is not on that list, which lets the test domain pass. The article notes that a future Chromium release could close the gap.

The piece places the issue in the wider history of internationalised domain names, which the IETF allowed in order to support non-Latin scripts. Those same scripts contain many visually similar characters, which makes detection hard. A 2020 study cited in the article found Chromium caught 64.1% of lookalike attempts, with Firefox and Safari behind it. Chromium underpins Chrome, Edge and Brave.

The researchers advise companies worried about impersonation to register lookalike domains and to encourage passkey use, since passkeys are tied to a specific domain and will not work on a fake site. The article suggests that no rule set can fully solve the problem, so defence will remain a matter of layered measures.

key_points: A coupler is simply two RJ45 sockets joined together and does not boost signal.
Each extra join is a potential failure point, causing dropouts or falling back to 100 Mbps.

stories.story:
Engadget offers practical advice for anyone whose Ethernet cable has become too short after moving a desk or equipment. A small RJ45 coupler can join two cables together without needing power or configuration, and a good-quality coupler should not noticeably slow a connection. However, the article argues that the coupler adds a connection that can fail, particularly if it is cheap or easily knocked.

Symptoms of a poor join can include occasional dropouts, transmission errors, or a link that falls back from 1 Gbps to 100 Mbps. The advice is to test with a good cable without the coupler before troubleshooting the router or contacting an internet provider. A coupler also does not extend the length limit, which is 100 metres for copper Ethernet including patch cords.

The article cites testing by trueCABLE using a Fluke DSX-8000 tester on Cat6 and Cat6A cables. Configurations with three couplers generally passed, one only marginally, while those with four failed. The results depend on the specific parts used, but they suggest that adding joins unnecessarily is a poor idea.

For a permanent setup, the recommendation is a single cable of the right length, routed with some slack. Where a cable already runs to a room with several devices, a small unmanaged switch is the better choice, since each port creates a separate link with its own distance limit. Anyone installing a camera or wireless access point should also check for Power over Ethernet support, as a standard switch will not supply power.

stories.claim: US Supreme Court justices appeared inclined to back a viewer's wider reading of the Video Privacy Protection Act against Paramount.
stories.summary: During oral argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, the US Supreme Court justices appeared open to a broad reading of the Video Privacy Protection Act. The plaintiff says a Paramount website sent his video viewing history to Facebook via Meta's Pixel without consent, and seeks a class action with damages of up to $2,500 per person. Paramount's lawyer argued the law was designed for video rentals, not web advertising. A ruling is expected by next summer.
key_points: The justices heard arguments in Salazar v. Paramount Global and appeared receptive to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff says Meta's Pixel sent his video history to Facebook without consent.
He seeks a class action with damages of up to $2,500 per person.

stories.story:
The US Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday in Salazar v. Paramount Global, a case that could widen privacy liability for websites that use tracking tools on video pages. According to reports cited in the article, the justices appeared inclined to side with the plaintiff, while Paramount's case did not seem to persuade them.

The plaintiff alleges that a Meta tracking tool known as the Pixel on a Paramount website sent details of the videos he watched to Facebook without his consent. He wants to bring a class action seeking up to $2,500 per person under the Video Privacy Protection Act, a 1988 law passed after a journalist published the video rental history of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork.

Paramount's lawyer, Paul Clement, argued that the plaintiff's reading would turn a law about video rentals into a sweeping internet privacy regime, and warned that sites might have to put videos behind consent walls. Justice Kagan suggested websites had two simple options, obtaining consent or stopping the sale of private data. Justice Sotomayor said gating videos would leave the choice to users. Justice Kavanaugh questioned whether it was right to repurpose a video law for web advertising tracking, and said consent would be over-broad.

stories.headline: 300-plus local data center bans have only delayed just three US projects
stories.claim: A SemiAnalysis report says over 300 local data centre moratoriums have delayed only a small share of planned US capacity.
stories.summary: SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data centre moratoriums have had little effect on US buildout, with only about 2.3 GW of 21 GW in moratorium areas likely to be delayed. Its 2027 forecast of 38 GW has barely moved in 12 months. The firm says moratoriums would need to be far more widespread and restrictive to slow the buildout. It also flags a Texas state-level pause on permits as a factor it has not fully counted.
key_points: Only about 2.3 GW of 21 GW in moratorium areas is likely to be delayed, according to SemiAnalysis.
The 2027 US data centre IT capacity forecast stands at 38 GW, more than double 2026.
Over 400 local moratorium measures are tracked across 17 states as of September.
Moratoriums often miss the site, permit or timeline, and do not revoke existing approvals.
A Texas Commission on Environmental Quality pause on data centre permits is not included in the 2.3 GW figure.
Public opinion in an August poll was more negative than positive about data centres.
stories.story:
A report from SemiAnalysis, shared on X and summarised by Tom's Hardware, argues that more than 300 local data centre construction moratoriums have done little to slow the US buildout. Of about 21 GW of data centre capacity located in moratorium areas, the firm estimates only around 2.3 GW is likely to be delayed. Its forecast of 38 GW of US data centre IT capacity for 2027, more than double 2026, has barely moved over the past year.

The firm defines a moratorium as a temporary legal pause, usually a freeze on accepting new applications. It tracks more than 400 local measures across 17 states, including some permanent zoning bans. New York, Texas, Pennsylvania and Oregon all acted within under two months this summer. The analysis found that moratoriums often do not reach the parcel, overlap the timeline or cover a project's use, and they do not revoke existing approvals. Michigan, for example, has 45 enacted moratoriums but effectively no pipeline exposure.

The report also highlights a Texas state pause. Governor Greg Abbott told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits for data centre projects, and law firm Bracewell expects it to last until the grid operator ERCOT completes its review in mid-December. The 2.3 GW figure excludes this pause, so the analysis may understate the effect. The article says the firm would be more worried by a strict state-level moratorium that also blocked off-grid projects.

SemiAnalysis concludes that moratoriums could delay the buildout but are not yet at scale. An Economist reporter quoted in the piece described them as much more bark than bite for now, with the bigger risk being a deterrent to newer projects. Public sentiment is also a factor, with an August poll by the firm showing more negative than positive views of data centres. The next checkpoint is a TCEQ compliance report to the governor's office.
stories.market_take: The analysis suggests the US data centre buildout is largely intact, though the Texas permit pause is a watch point for energy and infrastructure names.

stories.headline: Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line
stories.claim: Anthropic is lobbying for an AI safety bill that would let the government block model releases only for risks of over $1bn damage or over 50 casualties.
stories.summary: Politico reports that Anthropic is lobbying for a federal AI safety bill that would allow the government to block a model's release only when it poses a risk of $1 billion in damages or killing or injuring over 50 people. An independent third-party evaluator registered with the Commerce Department would assess the lab. Anthropic says the bill reflects its Advanced AI Framework. The article places the proposal against recent AI safety concerns and congressional proposals.
key_points: The bill would allow blocking a model release only if risk exceeds $1 billion in damages or harm to over 50 people.
Covered risks include bioweapons, AI-enabled cyberattacks and loss of control over AI models or agents.
An independent evaluator registered with the Commerce Department would review the lab periodically.
Evaluators must report potential risks within 72 hours, and a federal court in DC would decide on any halt.
Anthropic says the bill reflects its Advanced AI Framework, advocated since June.

stories.story:
Politico, as cited by Tom's Hardware, reports that Anthropic is lobbying for an AI safety bill that would give the US government power to block an AI model's release only in narrow circumstances. The threshold is a risk of at least $1 billion in damages, or the killing or injuring of more than 50 people. An independent third party registered with the Department of Commerce would evaluate the lab and its models periodically, and the lab could pay for those evaluations as long as this did not compromise the evaluator's independence.

The proposal names three categories of risk: the creation or release of a bioweapon, AI-enabled or AI-assisted cyberattacks, and an AI lab losing control of a model or agents. If an evaluator sees a possible such event, it must report to the Commerce Department within 72 hours. The department would then present the evidence to a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia, who would decide whether the release should be halted. The bill would also bar other departments, agencies or officers from ordering an AI lab to stop releasing a model.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has pushed with federal and state lawmakers since June, and described the policies as sensible. The article places the proposal in a climate of growing concern about AI safety, citing reported incidents involving OpenAI models, comments from Anthropic's chief executive about botnet risks, and a congressional proposal to require kill switches on the most powerful models.

The piece also mentions a separate proposal from Senator Bernie Sanders that would impose a 20-year prison term for developing AI superintelligence. The Anthropic bill would be one more measure for Congress to consider, and it is not yet law. The article does not give a timetable for a vote.
stories.market_take: Any federal AI safety rules could affect AI developers, though the proposal is at an early stage.

The agents coordinated by splitting tasks, warning of threats and recovering items from dead teammates.

stories.story:
Google's DeepMind team has reported that four AI agents running on the Gemini 4 Argon model completed Minecraft for the first time without any human input. The agents were placed in a randomly generated world with no assigned roles, strategies or game-specific tools. Over the course of the run they divided the work among themselves, warned one another about threats, retrieved items from teammates who had died and recorded their errors in a shared memory store. The session ended with the Ender Dragon defeated, which is the game's final boss.

The run was long and messy. It lasted 27 hours and 14 minutes and involved 2,783 JavaScript programs written by the agents, 229 chat messages between them and 605 deaths in total. The article estimates the session would have cost $1,620 at the standard Gemini 4 Argon price, which is due to take effect in 2027 rather than now.

The achievement is part of a wider pattern. The article notes that only a few years ago, video game performance of this kind typically required specialised AI systems trained from scratch for a single game. Now general-purpose agentic models are increasingly managing similar tasks. The report is a demonstration rather than a commercial product launch, and it does not say whether the approach will be released to the public. Readers should treat the cost figure as an estimate based on a future price.

stories.headline: Skip Intel Googlebooks for now, because your favorite apps and games may run poorly on them
stories.claim: Google says 96.6% of the top Android apps run on Intel Googlebooks, while Intel and Google dispute the cause of compatibility gaps.
stories.summary: Google and Intel are publicly disagreeing over app performance on Intel-based Googlebooks, a line of Android laptops. Google says a small number of complex apps, mainly games using Arm-only native code, need developer tuning, and that 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used apps run without issues on Intel Googlebooks. Intel responded by pointing to its Intel Bridge Technology translation layer and said it expects strong compatibility and fast performance. The article explains that Arm-based Snapdragon Googlebooks avoid translation, while Intel models must translate Arm instructions in real time, which can reduce frame rates in demanding native apps. The article advises buyers to check processor type before purchase.
key_points: Google says 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used Android apps run without issues on Intel Googlebooks.
Just over 300 popular apps are unavailable, mostly because they do not suit large screens, Google says.
Intel says its Intel Bridge Technology translation layer is built on ChromeOS technology without a virtual machine.
Dell and HP use Qualcomm Arm chips, while Acer, ASUS and Lenovo use Intel Panther Lake x86 chips.
Native Arm code in some games must be translated on Intel chips, which can cut frame rates.
Demanding games and emulators are likely to be the weakest spots on Intel models.
stories.story:
Google and Intel have publicly traded views on whether Android apps run well on Googlebooks, the Android-based laptops launched in October 2026. Google told Android Authority that most Android apps run smoothly on both Intel and Qualcomm models, but that a small number of complex apps or games need developer tuning on Intel hardware. It said it is working with developers, Intel and Qualcomm to improve compatibility. In a later statement it put a figure on the issue, saying 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used apps run without problems on Intel Googlebooks.

Intel responded to Gizmodo by stressing its Intel Bridge Technology. It said the translation layer uses the same underlying technology as ChromeOS but without a virtualised runtime, and that it expects users to see strong app compatibility and fast performance. The chipmaker credited its work on the Android framework and its Linux and open-source expertise. The article notes that about 300 popular apps are unavailable on Intel models, though Google says most of these are missing because they do not work on large screens rather than because of the chip.

The disagreement comes down to chip architecture. Android was built around Arm processors, and many apps, particularly games, contain native code compiled only for Arm. Dell and HP Googlebooks use Qualcomm's Arm-based Snapdragon X Elite, which runs this code directly. Acer, ASUS and Lenovo models use Intel's x86-based Panther Lake chips, which must translate Arm instructions in real time. On older Intel Chromebooks this approach felt sluggish, and the new Googlebook system removes the virtual machine but keeps the translation step. Apps written in Java or Kotlin generally run without trouble, so the issue mainly affects performance-heavy native code.

For buyers, the practical advice is to check the processor before purchase. Everyday tasks and streaming should be fine on Intel models, while demanding games such as Genshin Impact and emulators may struggle. Both companies are expected to release updates to narrow the gaps, though the timing is not stated.
stories.market_take: The dispute could slightly weigh on Intel's Googlebook appeal against Qualcomm-based models.

stories.headline: World Bank backs ‘small AI’ on phones for poorer nations, Guardian reports
stories.claim: The World Bank is encouraging developing countries to adopt compact 'small AI' models that run on basic phones.
stories.summary: The World Bank's chief knowledge officer, Paschal Donohoe, has urged developing countries to build 'small AI', which are compact, task-specific models that run on phones with weak signals. He said such tools could speed up growth in emerging economies if they fit local needs and languages. He gave the example of Indian farmers needing soil analysis in their own language. The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva said governments must first provide power, digital infrastructure and protection from bad actors. The article also notes large infrastructure gaps and warns that AI could change or remove 40% of jobs worldwide over time.
key_points: Donohoe says compact 'small AI' models should run on phones with weak signals and in local languages.
He argues AI could bring growth within decades that might otherwise take centuries.
Indian farmers in the World Bank's AgriConnect scheme are cited as a use case for soil analysis.
IMF chief Georgieva says power, digital infrastructure and protection from misuse must come first.
Georgieva warned 40% of jobs could be changed or removed by AI over time, with entry-level roles most at risk.
The World Bank says it raised $120bn in private capital over the past year as some rich countries cut aid.
stories.story:
The World Bank wants developing countries to focus on what it calls 'small AI': compact models trained on narrow data for a single task, which can run on a mobile phone even when the signal is weak. Paschal Donohoe, the bank's chief knowledge officer and a former Irish finance minister, said the technology could speed up growth in emerging economies, provided it suits local needs. He suggested that development that might once have taken centuries could happen within decades.

Donohoe gave the example of farmers in India within the bank's AgriConnect scheme, who need soil analysis in their own language. He argued there will never be enough agricultural experts to serve every small farm, and said such products could come from the World Bank, governments and private firms working together. The remarks followed discussions on AI at the World Bank and IMF meetings in Bangkok earlier this month.

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said governments must first put in place power, digital infrastructure and protection from bad actors. She argued that if these basics are in place, AI adoption could be as democratic as the mobile phone. The gaps are large, however. A World Bank report from August found almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa had no electricity. Georgieva also warned that around 40% of jobs worldwide could be changed or eliminated by AI over time, with young people starting out facing the greatest risk as entry-level roles shrink.

Donohoe said the bank had raised $120bn in private capital over the past year at a time when countries including the US and UK have reduced aid budgets. The article is based on a Guardian report and the remarks are policy aspirations rather than announced programmes with set funding.

stories.story:
A report says Nvidia is developing a custom form of high-bandwidth memory, called NVHBM, and has asked the major memory makers to change how they build it. Under the proposal, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix would make the base die of the memory stack on TSMC's 3nm process, rather than each using their own process. The core die would use the sixth-generation 1c DRAM process. The idea is that one common base die would make performance more consistent and mean Nvidia does not need to separately verify each supplier's samples, saving time.

According to the report, Samsung has agreed, which would be a notable change for a company that has traditionally developed its HBM core and base dies in-house. Samsung is reportedly still keeping its own foundry as an option in case demand for NVHBM exceeds TSMC's production capacity. Standard HBM development would continue within Samsung. The article also says Nvidia has claimed the custom design could deliver up to 30% more memory bandwidth than standard HBM4E while drawing up to 15% less power.
